# nsite-clay

> A self-editable nsite. One HTML file holds a page's markup, styling, content
> and state, and republishes itself: the browser serialises the document, stores
> it on Blossom, and publishes a NIP-5A manifest pointing at it. Relays hold the
> manifest, Blossom holds the bytes, and there is no server in between.

This file is for agents. If you are building someone a website with nsite-clay,
read this first and follow it. It tells you what to ask, what to decide, and
where the details are. It does not repeat the documentation.

- Human walkthrough: https://npub12edc7326qsryw5rw5yw0yh57fmj9r8jf4c8xazz6333w305qgnms9ypvj2.nsite.lol/docs.html
- Runtime reference: https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay/blob/main/docs/RUNTIME-API.md
- Templates: https://npub12edc7326qsryw5rw5yw0yh57fmj9r8jf4c8xazz6333w305qgnms9ypvj2.nsite.lol/templates.html
- Source: https://github.com/jooray/nsite-clay
- What an nsite is: https://nsite.run

## What you are actually building

One `index.html`. It links two files from the site root and nothing else:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/nsite-clay-base.css">
<script src="/nsite-clay.js"></script>
<script src="/nsite-clay-chrome.js"></script>
```

Your job is the markup, the styling and the words. Sign-in, saving, versions,
media upload, feeds and the composer already exist. Writing your own is the
commonest mistake: check the runtime reference before you implement anything.

## Start from a template

Do not start from a blank file. Ten templates cover the usual shapes:

`event` `blog` `project` `personal` `links` `gallery` `terminal` `phrack`
`brutal` `eco`

```bash
npx nsite-clay init mysite --template=blog --npub=npub1…
```

Pick by what the page is for, not by which looks nicest, then redesign it. The
template gives you a working page with the chrome wired up; the design is yours
to change. Change the CSS variables on `:root` first, because the shared
toolbar follows them, and only then write your own rules.

Read `templates/_shared/CONTRACT.md` in the repo before editing one. It is
short and it is binding.

## What to ask the person

Four things, and you can usually infer three of them.

1. **Their npub.** Required. It goes in `nc:owner` and it is the only key that
   can ever change the page. If they do not have one, they need a Nostr key
   before anything else works.
2. **What the page is for.** This picks the template.
3. **What should come from Nostr.** Their notes, their articles, their photos,
   somebody else's. Feeds are markup: `nc:feed="articles" nc:authors="npub1…"`.
4. **Whether anyone else needs to edit it.** The answer is no. One key writes
   the document; there is no shared editing. Say so early rather than building
   toward it.

Do not ask for their nsec. You do not need it and you should not have it.

## Getting it online

```bash
npx nsite-clay deploy mysite --sec=nsec1…          # a raw key
NOSTR_BUNKER_URI="bunker://…" npx nsite-clay deploy mysite   # a remote signer
```

Prefer the bunker. It keeps the key off the machine running the deploy, which
matters when that machine is yours rather than theirs. Pass the URI in the
environment, never as an argument: an argument is visible to every process on
the box.

The page lands at `https://<their npub>.nsite.lol/`. Other gateways serve the
same site from the same events: `nsite.lol`, `nsite.run`, `nosto.re`, `nwb.tf`,
`nsite.cloud`, `shakespeare.to`. A CNAME at any of them gives a custom domain.

After the first deploy the page publishes itself, and they never need a
terminal again. Tell them that.

## Signing in: recommend a remote signer

Three ways in. Steer them to the second.

1. **A NIP-07 browser extension.** Fine on their own machine.
2. **A remote signer over NIP-46**, Amber on Android or nsec.app. The key stays
   on their phone and every save is approved there. This is the right default
   for a page served by a gateway, and it is what you should suggest first.
3. **Pasting a key into the page.** It works, it stays in the tab, and it is
   written nowhere. It is still the weakest option and you should say so rather
   than defaulting to it.

The toolbar handles all three. You do not write sign-in code.

## The edit gate

Every template ships with `nc:edit-gate="hash"` on `<html>`. Readers see the
page and nothing to click. The owner adds `#edit` to the URL and the toolbar
appears.

Tell them this explicitly, because a page with no visible way in looks broken
to someone who has forgotten. Their editing URL is:

```
https://<their npub>.nsite.lol/#edit
```

Worth putting in the handover note. `nc.settings.open()` turns the gate off if
they would rather have the toolbar always visible.

## Autosave is off, deliberately

Every save stores the whole page again and files a version, so saving on a
timer publishes a dozen versions of one paragraph. Leave it off unless they ask.
Leaving the page with unsaved work already warns them.

## Customising a template

Work in this order. It saves rewriting.

1. **The variables.** `--nc-ink`, `--nc-bg`, `--nc-panel`, `--nc-edge`,
   `--nc-accent`, `--nc-radius`, `--nc-chrome-font`, `--nc-mono`. Setting these
   restyles the toolbar, the dialogs and the feeds at once.
2. **The content.** Real words. Everything a person would plausibly change gets
   `editable` (a container, where Enter makes a paragraph) or
   `editable="single-line"` (a heading, a caption, a row).
3. **The layout and type.** Your own rules, under the variables.
4. **The feeds.** Style `.nc-item`, `.nc-title`, `.nc-by`, `.nc-summary`. Do not
   change what the feed emits; change how it looks.

If you insert markup while the page is being edited, call
`nc.editable.refresh()` before focusing it, or the new region will not be
typeable.

Never copy `nsite-clay.js` or `nsite-clay-base.css` into the site. They live at
the root so that one upgrade fixes every page.

## Things that will bite you

- **A save must not reference a file the manifest does not list.** The runtime
  refuses to publish that, and the error names the file. Deploy the whole
  directory with the CLI rather than hand-editing the path table.
- **Assets are content-fingerprinted.** `/logo-9f2a1e.png` changes when the file
  changes. Do not hardcode a fingerprint you saw once.
- **Relays disagree.** Publish to several, and include `wss://relay.nsite.lol`
  so the gateway sees changes promptly.
- **Blossom servers are picky.** Several refuse `text/html`. `cdn.hzrd149.com`
  and `blossom.primal.net` work.
- **Feeds are fetched, not stored.** A save keeps the widget's configuration and
  none of the posts, so a reader with scripting off sees an empty block. Design
  for that.
- **One key, no conflict detection.** Two devices editing at once lose one
  side's work.

## Writing

The words matter more than the design and they are the part most often left as
filler. No em or en dashes. No "there are several ways to". No sentence that
announces what the next sentence will do. Write what the page is, for someone
who has not seen it.

If the page is in a language other than English, write it as a native speaker
would, with that language's punctuation and typography, not English rules in
translated words.

## Handing it over

Tell them, in this order: the address of their page, the same address with
`#edit`, which key controls it, and that the page now updates itself. That is
the whole operating manual.
